metadata.content: Thunder is a Deno-based full-stack web framework with file-based routing, a hooks system, and MongoDB integration. The project commonly contains routes/, hooks/, plugins/, schemas/, scripts/, workers/, public/, core/, serve.ts, serve.base.ts, database.ts, .env, and deno.json. The core/ directory contains framework internals and must not be modified.

Files directly inside routes/ become routes: routes/users.ts handles /users/*, routes/posts.ts handles /posts/*, and routes/index.ts handles /. Subfolders inside routes/ are ignored by route discovery. For example, routes/admin/users.ts is not registered. Subfolders may still be used for code organization.

Thunder is designed for serverless environments. Do not use background jobs or long-running processes in the application. Keep requests stateless, optimize cold starts, and create database indexes through scripts rather than during application startup. Deploy asynchronous workers separately when needed.
Thunder provides VS Code snippets: router scaffolds a router file, req scaffolds a validated route handler, model scaffolds a database schema/model, and crud scaffolds a complete CRUD operation.

Router functions and route handler preparation functions must be named functions, not arrow functions. Correct usage includes new Router("/api/", function users(router) { ... }) and router.get("/", function listUsers() { ... }). Arrow functions in these positions can cause errors. Handler names must also be unique within a router.

Route handlers use a prepare pattern. The outer named function runs once during route registration, while the returned function handles each request. Define schemas and other reusable preparation logic in the outer function rather than recreating them for every request.

The shape() function registers request and response validators. Shapes enable runtime validation, OpenAPI generation through deno task generate:openapi, and TypeScript SDK generation through deno task generate:sdk. A route can return an object containing shape and handler functions.

Available router methods are router.get, router.post, router.put, router.patch, router.del, and router.all. Use del rather than delete for DELETE routes. Path parameters use path-to-regexp syntax, including :id, :id?, {/*path} for wildcards, and {/:id} for optional segments.

Router groups are shared labels across related route files, not unique names for individual files. Multiple files may intentionally use .group("Blog") so their endpoints appear together in generated OpenAPI specifications and SDKs. Grouped files can be colocated in a folder, but route subfolders are not registered and do not affect URL prefixes.

Response helpers are imported from @/core/http/response.ts. Available helpers include Response.ok(), Response.json(value), Response.created(value), Response.badRequest(), Response.unauthorized(), Response.forbidden(), Response.notFound(), and Response.redirect(path). Use these helpers rather than manually constructing equivalent responses.

Hooks intercept requests before and after handlers. Place hook files in hooks/. Hook priority determines execution order: higher numbers execute first. Priority 100 is suitable for security and authentication, priorities 3 and 2 for validation or rate limiting, priority 1 for late processing, and negative priorities such as -100 for logging and cleanup.

A hook pre function runs before a handler and may return a Response to short-circuit processing, or return void to continue. A post function runs afterward and may return a Response to replace the original response. Hook context includes req, res for post hooks, scope for the router name, and name for the handler name.

For a brand-new project created from the Thunder template, run deno task init. This is destructive: it removes existing Git history, initializes a fresh repository, runs setup, and configures environment files. For a cloned or forked existing repository, run deno task setup instead; setup configures Git settings and hooks without changing history.

A typical setup creates .env with DATABASE_URL, optionally installs the official core plugin, and starts development with deno task dev. Example:
git clone https://github.com/Huruf-Tech/thunder.git my-app
cd my-app
deno task init
echo "DATABASE_URL=mongodb://localhost:27017/my-db" > .env
deno task add:plugin -n Huruf-Tech/thunder-core
deno task dev

Supported environment files are .env, .env.development, .env.production, and .env.test. DATABASE_URL is required for the database connection. ENV_TYPE identifies the environment. Plugin-specific variables are documented by each plugin.
Manual indexes reduce cold-start time, avoid repeated initialization work in serverless instances, provide predictable performance, and make database operations explicit for developers.

Foreign-reference fields must not end with Id or Ids. Name fields after the referenced entity: user, tenant, category, users, categories, or tags. Use metadata such as $objectId.meta({ ref: "users" }) to identify references. Thunder uses these names to infer foreign references and lets generated SDKs populate related objects on demand.

createCRUD generates POST /users/api for creation, GET /users/api for listing, GET /users/api/:id for retrieval, GET /users/api/count for counting, PATCH /users/api/:id for updates, and DELETE /users/api/:id for deletion. Specific operations can be disabled with the disable option.

Thunder does not support built-in background jobs because serverless functions do not provide persistent connections or long-running processes. Use a separate worker server, a managed queue such as BullMQ, or a MongoDB-backed queue.

Use the @/ alias for project imports. Correct examples include import { Router } from "@/core/http/router.ts", import { Env } from "@/core/utils/env.ts", and import { mongodb } from "@/database.ts". Avoid relative imports for core modules and database files.

Code should use TypeScript strict mode, named exports for utilities, default exports for routers and hooks, async/await instead of promise chains, Zod schemas in the prepare phase, Response helpers, and validation before processing. Avoid comments that merely explain obvious code.

Before writing helper code or installing a dependency, check Thunder's built-in utilities. Reuse Env, Logger, cache, createHash, queryAsJson, parseQueryParams, paginated, ejsRender, handlebarsRender, createCRUD, paramsAsJson, bodyAsJson, parseBasicAuth, serveAssets, Response helpers, and Zod. Prefer mapped Deno standard-library packages over arbitrary npm packages.

Never edit core/ or plugins/. These directories are managed and overwritten by update commands. Add application behavior in routes/, hooks/, schemas/, scripts/, workers/, or other project files. Extend behavior with hooks or wrappers instead of changing framework or plugin source.

Update the framework with deno task update:core. Commit or stash application work first, run the update, then run deno task check and verify the application with deno task dev. Update an installed plugin with deno task update:plugin -n org/plugin-name.

Thunder uses a unified project-plugin architecture: a Thunder project can itself be installed as a plugin. Plugins live under plugins/{org}/{name}/, and their routes and hooks are automatically merged with the main application. Install with deno task add:plugin -n org/plugin-name.

Plugin setup is not automatic when a plugin is installed. Use deno task add:plugin -n org/plugin-name --setup or run deno task setup:plugin -n org/plugin-name afterward. Setup can create indexes, seed data, or run migrations against selected environments.

The official thunder-core plugin provides authentication through better-auth, RBAC, security headers, CORS, an admin user-management panel, session management, database migrations, and utilities such as withAuthSession, withTenant, and withAuthGuard.

A plugin has the same basic structure as a Thunder project. It may contain routes/, hooks/, schemas/, lib/, scripts/, types/, serve.ts, database.ts, deno.json, .env.example, README.md, llms.txt, and PLUGIN_GUIDE.md. Plugin route files should use semantic namespaces such as /stripe or /email.

Plugin lifecycle scripts are scripts/setupPlugin.ts and scripts/cleanupPlugin.ts. Setup is for indexes, seed data, and migrations; cleanup is for teardown. Thunder runs the selected script once per environment with ENV_TYPE set appropriately. If a script is absent, the operation is a safe no-op.

Lifecycle scripts should be idempotent. Index creation is naturally idempotent, while seed insertion should use unique indexes or upserts. Keep actual work in importable functions and allow scripts to run directly. Use Promise.allSettled when independent index operations should not abort one another.

Plugin setup and cleanup commands accept comma-separated environments such as development, production, and test:
deno task add:plugin -n org/plugin-name --setup=development,production
deno task setup:plugin -n org/plugin-name --envs=development
deno task remove:plugin -n org/plugin-name --clean=development,production
The corresponding environment files must contain DATABASE_URL and required plugin variables.

Plugin hooks should follow priority conventions: 100 or higher for authentication and security, 50–99 for business logic, 0–49 for optional hooks, and -100 for logging or cleanup. Plugins should be composable, independently testable, semantically namespaced, documented with environment variables, and versioned with semantic versioning.

Multiple plugins can be installed together. Their routes and hooks are merged automatically. For example, thunder-core may provide /auth/* and /users/*, a Stripe plugin may provide /stripe/*, and an email plugin may provide /email/*. Plugins currently cannot recursively depend on other plugins; consumers must install required plugins separately.

Common tasks include deno task init, deno task setup, deno task dev, deno task start, deno task check, deno task update:core, deno task generate:openapi, deno task generate:sdk, deno task generate:app, deno task add:plugin, deno task setup:plugin, deno task update:plugin, and deno task remove:plugin.

Authentication middleware can be implemented as a priority-100 pre hook. Read the Bearer token from Authorization, return Response.unauthorized() when absent or invalid, verify it, and expose the authenticated user identifier to handlers, for example by setting an X-User-Id request header.

denoConfig is an already-resolved object, not a function. Import denoConfig, readDenoConfig, and denoConfigPath from @/core/utils/denoConfig.ts. Use denoConfig.name or denoConfig.tasks for the current project. Use await readDenoConfig(path) for another configuration, or pass true as the second argument to read statically without import caching.

Hash utilities use Web Crypto asynchronously and Node crypto synchronously. Import createHash, createHashBase64, createHashSync, createHashBase64Sync, and SupportedHashAlg from @/core/utils/hash.ts. These produce digests only and have no verify helper. They are not suitable for password storage without salting; use a dedicated password KDF.
